en: The ritual of offering consists briefly of twenty-four rules:
Prostrate before Vairocana Buddha, whose pure eyes are blossomed like blue lotuses.
Relying upon the Mahāvairocana Sūtra-king, I shall explain the various ritual procedures for making offerings;
so that the methods of mantra may be accomplished in their proper sequence, and one may swiftly attain realization as described therein,
and furthermore, so that the fundamental mind may be freed from defilement, I now briefly proclaim these essentials.
Next, regarding the first point of selecting the site for the Dharma:
In a location appropriate to the specific terrain, amidst the valleys and ridges of wondrous mountains,
within various grottoes between two peaks— one shall find stability at all times.
Water lilies, lotuses, and blue lotuses adorn the ponds everywhere;
by the banks of great rivers and streams, far removed from the clamor of crowds and people, stand trees with spreading branches that delight the mind.
Abounding in milky trees and auspicious grasses, they are free from mosquitoes, gadflies, cold, and heat.
May there be no hindrances from fierce beasts, venomous insects, or various obstacles.
Having frequented in the past temples, stupas, hermitages, and ancient sages’ caves, one should dwell in a place that accords with one’s own mind’s inclination;
having abandoned the household life, one cuts off all clamor and worldly affairs.
Diligently turning away from the five desires and all fetters and obscurations, he single-mindedly and deeply delights in the flavor of the Dharma;
having nurtured his mind, he completes the *Siddhi-sādhana-dharma*.
If one obtains a site as previously described, one must first perform ablutions. For bathing, there is a mudrā and a mantra; the mantra should be recited three times: "LĀM VĀM.

Once the mudrā has been formed with the hands, turn to the right to protect one's own body and turn to the left to expel all māras. Subsequently, point toward the eight directions as well as above and below. This concludes the ritual for bathing.
If one digs the earth, one must likewise employ the secret mudrā and mantra. The mantra should be recited three times as follows:

“Namaḥ samantabuddhānām ha. This mantra and mudrā, or those explained in other sūtras, may be used interchangeably without contradiction; if one can understand and apply them with skillful mastery, all undertakings will be accomplished.
Next, when molding the earth, one must likewise employ the secret mudrā and mantra.

The mantra is: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānām khaṃ*. This should be recited three times. If you wish to consecrate the ground, first enter the heart of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātucitta*) to purify the mundane world. At the very bottom, establish the great space; from space arises the wind-circle (*vāyumaṇḍala*), and so on, up to the earth-circle (*pṛthivīmaṇḍala*), which one should visualize as being equal to the ocean of fragrant water.

Next, if one wishes to measure the ground: standing at the northeast corner, measure southward; from the southeast corner, measure to the southwest corner; from that point, measure to the northwest corner; and from the north, return to the original location. Once the measurement of the ground is completed as described above.
For all ritual implements of offering, follow the sequence of daily rotations listed previously; furthermore, the wrathful forms are accompanied by both joy and anger.

When performing the recitation, from the first watch until the third, and from the fourth watch until midnight, prefix with *HŪṂ* (𑖬), *KHAṂ* (𑖮), *PHAṬ* (𑖥), and *OṂ* (𑖀) at the beginning and end; at the conclusion, add *HŪṂ* (𑖬), *KHAṂ* (𑖮), and *PHAṬ* (𑖥). At the commencement of the speech, one should empower the position of the fundamental mind (*mūlacitta*).
For subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), the empowerment is transferred to the tip of the *ūrṇā-kośa* (white tuft of hair).

For summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*), it resides at the syllable-gateway *HĀ*; its color is like the light of fire. This syllable-gateway *HAṂ* is dark blue-black in color and is placed upon the wind element. This syllable-gateway *A* is the color of refined gold. Adding this syllable-gateway *VAṂ*, its color is like the white moonlight; when held at the lower part of the body, it is called the yoga-seat.
For the Holder of the Self-Navel, it is the auspicious seat; for the Increaser, the śrīvatsa seat;
and for the One Who Pacifies Calamities, the lotus seat.
If at the beginning or end of a mantra there are *namaḥ*,
when reciting it, place the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning and add *svāhā* at the end.
At that time, from the latter part of the night until the sun first rises, one should maintain the practice of recitation;
from midday until sunset, one should maintain a countenance of joy and a mind of serene detachment.
Next, when the ritual procedures are completed, one should sit facing the *maṇḍala*.
The mantra for entering the Buddha-samaya is as follows:

*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ āsme tṛsme samaye svāhā.* One should then bind the Samaya-mudrā, which is said to purify the three karmas. By touching all the limbs with it and reciting this word of truth (*satyavākya*), the mere binding of this secret mudrā is able to purify the stage of the Tathāgata.
Next, one binds the *dharmadhātujāta*, the emblem of secret wisdom. Because it purifies body, speech, and mind, it is rotated throughout the entire body.
The mantra should be recited three times:

*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ damadadatu sarvabodhi*. Contemplate one’s own body as being like the self-nature of the *dharmadhātu*, or else proclaim it by repeating the words of truth (*satyavākya*) three times.
One should perceive oneself as abiding in the essence of phenomena, stainless like space.
Next, one should adorn one's own body with the vajra armor; one should contemplate that the garments thus donned produce flames of light throughout the entire body.
The mantra is:

*Namaḥ samantabhadra-vajrāya oṃ vajrākaca vañca hūṃ*. To avoid all māras and eliminate one's own obstacles, one must recite this mantra; then, by visualizing the stainless syllable as well as other types of evil-minded beings, they will all scatter in the four directions upon seeing it.
Next, for the confession of all roots of transgression, one must contemplate the syllable-gateway *Ḥraṃ*, which is colored like the rising sun, burning away sins from beginningless time.
The mantra is as follows:

“Namaḥ sarvathāgatebhyo viśvamukhebhyaḥ | Svāhā khaṃ udgate saprahe | Gaganakheṭa svāhā. With this mantra and mudrā, one places it upon the crown of the head and applies it to the five limbs, along with incense, flowers, lamps, ointments, powdered incense, and all other exquisite offerings—both mundane and supramundane—which thereby become offerings of samādhi. All are performed with the mudrās and mantras; this constitutes the purification of the three karmas.

Next, one should bind the boundaries of all directions. Recite the mantra of Acala’s seal, along with the mantra for removing impurities and expelling obstacles, and the mantra for protecting oneself three times:

*Namaḥ samantabhadra vajranana mahāroṣaṇe sphoṭaya hūṃ trāka haṃ mam.* With the *samādhi-hand* (left hand) placed at the heart and the *prajñā-hand* (right hand) rotated universally, one should know that whatever object is touched is thereby purified. By rotating this [hand] counter-clockwise, the expulsion of obstacles is accomplished.
If one binds the boundaries of the cardinal and intermediate directions, one should cause them all to turn clockwise; all other remaining matters serve to extinguish evil and purify all obstacles.
Next, using mantras and mudrās, one should invoke the assembly of holy ones; as spoken by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, they shall come according to their original vows.
The mantra is:

Oṃ vajrasattvāya hūṃ hūṃ heye heye. By means of this, the Buddhas, the Saviors of the World, summon all those who abide on the ten stages and other bodhisattvas of great power, as well as other sentient beings with unruly and unwholesome minds.
Regarding the Wisdom Wind Banner: to recite it once and summon once is the invocation.
Next, one offers the samaya with mantras and mudrās; the characteristics of the mudrās are as observed above in the various samaya teachings.
The mantra is:

*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām asame trisame samaye svāhā*. This is the Buddha-samaya-mudrā. By means of such skillful means, one correctly demonstrates the samaya; thus, one will universally benefit all classes of sentient beings, attain siddhi, and swiftly fulfill unsurpassed vows, causing the lords of the original mantras and all vidyās to rejoice—thus one should make this aspiration.
Next, one should expel the various māras and hook the Honored One, then enter the Gate of Joy (Ratimukha) to cause the Honored One to give rise to joy, while reciting the mantra for expelling.

The mantra is: *HŪṂ NI SU-HŪṂ VA NI HŪṂ*. With the wisdom hand (*prajñā-hasta*), one wards off the followers of Māra; reciting the mantra and performing the mudrā, one turns to the left. With the concentration hand (*samādhi-hasta*), one forms the hook and retains [the deity]; this is the method for retaining the Honored One.
Next, offer the argha water.
The argha water to be offered has already been fully prepared; empower it with the mantra of the principal deity by reciting the following mantra fifteen times:
*maṃ saṃ maṃ svāhā*. "Offered to all the Sugatas, may it bathe their stainless bodies; next, it shall purify all those born from the mouth of the Buddha."
Next, present the Vajrāsana and perform the lotus mudrā; the mantra for seating [the deity] is:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām āḥ*. Place this everywhere where the Awakened One is to be seated.
Next, one should dispel the obstructions arising from oneself by means of the Great Wisdom Sword Mudrā and the mantra of the Noble Acala. The mantra is:

*Namaḥ samantabhadra-vajra-hūṃ vaṃ*. [Perform] the Immovable Sword Mudrā. One should visualize the most supreme vajra-flames, which incinerate all obstructions until none remain; the wise practitioner should then transform themselves into the body of Vajrasattva, with the mantra and mudrā in union pervading all limbs.

Next, recite the mantras repeatedly, each uttering their respective root mantra as well as the vidyā they personally uphold. Having performed this accordingly, one should offer them by calling their names; first, place them all pervasively within the mind of the pure dharmadhātu.
Regarding what is called the "Seal of the Immovable Sword of the Past," it is the syllable-gateway *raṃ* (囕).
It is to be employed as a secret seal at the time of offering unguents, as previously explained in the section on the offering of names.
The mantra is:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ viśuddha-ketu-udbhava svāhā*. Next, offer incense.
The mantra should be recited three times:
"Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ damadhatudhunvate svāhā. Next, offer a lamp.
The mantra should be recited three times:
"Namaḥ samantabuddhānām | Oṃ tathāgatārcisaparavāṇasvabhāvakāyakāraśodhani svāhā. Next, offer various foods and drinks as an offering.
The mantra is:

*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām | Arara karara maraṇi daraṇi mahāmari svāhā*. Next, regarding the other articles of offering that should be presented, one should purify and respectfully offer them to the assembly of noble deities according to this ritual procedure.

Furthermore, one performs the ritual of the mind, which is pure and most magnificent; all that is offered is fully complete, equal to the Dharma-realm, pervading this world and other lands, universally entering into all realms of existence.

Arising from the merit of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, there are banners, pennants, various necklaces, and canopies; vast and wondrous pavilions; as well as celestial jewel-tree kings, everywhere filled with all manner of requisites, such as clouds of various fragrances and flowers, boundless as space itself.
Each rains down various offerings to perform the service of making offerings for the attainment of Buddhahood; contemplating this, one presents them to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
By means of the *Ākāśagarbha-vidyā* and the Universal Offering Mudrā, performing the empowerment three times, all that is wished for shall be accomplished.

Next, regarding the Universal Seal (*samantamudrā*): wearing it upon the crown of the head, one performs extensive offerings and repents of all defilements. Following the ritual seat according to the primary method, one enters *samādhi* and, taking the primary seed-syllable, places it within one's own body, transforming it into the body of the deity.
The mantra is as follows, using the aforementioned general offering mudrā:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām ā*. Next, perform the recitation of the Dharma-mantra three lakṣas; the samādhi will then manifest before you, and you will transform into the body of the Dharma-realm.

Once the recitation is completed, entrust the count of repetitions to the Honored One; then, once again offer the argha water and other various articles of offering, performing them extensively according to the initial procedure, while protecting both the Honored One and yourself.

Once the ritual tasks are completed, loosen the *samaya* at the crown of the head to protect the *maṇḍala* and one’s own person. Then recite Mahāyāna scriptures, seal the stūpas, and bathe the Buddha images. When attending to worldly affairs, whether during the first or last watches of the night, the number of recitations remains the same; however, at noon, the count is reduced by half.
Regarding the methods for recitation, there are briefly two types:
first, based on time; second, based on signs.
"Based on time" refers to the completion of a predetermined number of recitations, as well as fixed durations such as days, months, or specific limits.

Regarding the signs: when a Buddha stūpa, image, or painting emits light, flames, sounds, and so forth, one should know that these are signs that the karmic obstructions of the practitioner of mantra have been purified.
When the ritual affairs are concluded, one should recite this verse, which says:
"All phenomena arise from conditions; These phenomena cease because of conditions.
That which arises from causes ceases; This is what the Great Śramaṇa has taught."

In constructing a maṇḍala, one follows the aforementioned method. Regarding its dimensions, it may be constructed according to one’s capacity, with the largest being thirty-six cubits, twenty-eight, sixteen, eight, six, or four; the smallest is two cubits. These measurements are all taken using the *hasta* (cubit) of a human male of normal stature, and the shape is as previously described.
If one is a king, a minister, or a householder, possessing various kinds of excellent items such as vessels made of the seven precious gems,
and if the ācārya has many disciples who are intelligent and sharp-witted, one should construct an extensive maṇḍala. However,

if the patron lacks these and there are no excellent offerings of the seven precious gems, nor are there many intelligent and sharp-witted disciples, one should perform the abbreviated rite according to what can be provided by one's means.

Regarding all items offered in worship, with the sole exception of the five pungent vegetables, alcohol, meat, and other impure things, the offering vessels should be made of gold, silver, copper, iron, or porcelain; all others are unsuitable for use. As for the various flavors and offerings within the altar, they should be replaced once every day; however, in the case of fruits and the like, it is also permissible to replace them once every three days.

Whenever one wishes to change the objects of offering or perform sweeping and cleaning, one must first dismiss the noble beings and inform the venerable countenance; only then should one sweep, clean, and make offerings of scented unguents.
The practitioner says aloud:
"May Your Honored Presence temporarily depart from the maṇḍala.
Having finished sweeping and wiping it clean, he applies fragrant paste, reopens the seats, and completes the formal invitation; the method for the offerings is as before.

Furthermore, in the center of the inner courtyard, there is one principal deity; whichever Buddha or other figure the patron prefers shall serve as the presiding lord of the maṇḍala. From the Prajñāpāramitā down to the Bodhisattvas and so forth, they are to be installed according to the patron's wishes, with the principal deity at their head.

The Ritual for Offerings, based on the Lingyun (Ryūun) edition: collated once on the twenty-third day of the fourth month in the third year of the Jōkyō era; punctuated by Netgen (Jōgen), who had served forty-eight years, after correcting what was decayed or missing.
